questions.prompt: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it fills. Starting empty, what is the amortized time per append over $n$ appends, assuming a copy or write costs $\Theta(1)$?

answers.explanation: The copied capacities form a geometric series $1+2+4+\cdots=O(n)$. Together with $n$ writes, the total cost is $\Theta(n)$, or $\Theta(1)$ per append.
The total work is linear, not cubic as this per-operation bound would imply.
Doubling capacity makes resizing infrequent; it does not cause exponential total copying.

answers.text: There is no finite amortized bound.
answers.explanation: Summing the geometric series gives a finite linear total cost.
A single resizing append can be linear, but that is a worst-case individual cost, not the amortized cost.
The total cost is linear, which yields a constant cost per append.
This overcounts copying: an old capacity is copied only when that capacity fills.
There are logarithmically many resizes, but the total copied elements form a geometric sum, not n times the number of resizes.
Every append performs at least one write; its amortized cost cannot decrease below a constant.

answers.text: Constant amortized time only if the append values are random.
answers.explanation: The bound holds for every sequence of append values; it is not a distributional average.

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, which property explains why breadth-first search finds a shortest path from its source to every reachable vertex?

answers.text: It explores vertices in nondecreasing distance from the source.
answers.explanation: BFS finishes distance layer k before exploring layer k+1. The first discovery of a vertex therefore uses a minimum number of edges.
BFS need not enumerate paths; it visits each reachable vertex once.

answers.text: It always chooses the smallest-numbered vertex.
answers.explanation: Vertex labels have no bearing on shortest-path distances.
This graph is unweighted; BFS uses a FIFO queue, not edge sorting.

answers.text: It explores one branch fully before backtracking.
answers.explanation: That describes depth-first search, which does not generally give shortest paths.

answers.text: It chooses a neighbor with the largest degree.
answers.explanation: Degree is unrelated to the minimum number of edges from the source.

answers.text: It keeps vertices in a last-in, first-out stack.
answers.explanation: A stack gives depth-first behavior. BFS relies on a first-in, first-out queue.

answers.text: It finalizes a vertex only after exploring all paths to it.
answers.explanation: The first discovery is sufficient because BFS explores distance layers in order.

answers.text: It visits vertices in nondecreasing degree.
answers.explanation: The invariant concerns distance from the source, not degree.

answers.text: It guarantees that every discovered edge lies on a shortest path from the source.
answers.explanation: BFS tree edges give shortest paths, but other graph edges can connect vertices in the same layer.

questions.prompt: A sorted array contains $n$ distinct values. What is the tight worst-case time bound for ordinary binary search, assuming constant-time array access?

answers.explanation: Each comparison discards roughly half of the remaining interval. After $k$ comparisons its size is about $n/2^k$, so $k=\Theta(\log n)$.
That is the worst-case bound for a linear scan. Binary search halves the search interval.
Binary search does not compare every pair of entries.
One comparison is enough in some cases, but not in the worst case as the array grows.
Halving the interval produces logarithmic, not square-root, growth.
That is a typical comparison-sorting bound; the array is already sorted.
The algorithm follows one shrinking interval, not an exponential search tree.
Repeated halving gives a logarithm. A double logarithm would require a much faster reduction.
Each of the logarithmically many comparisons costs constant time; there is no second logarithmic factor.
The relevant equation is the remaining interval size after repeated halving, not a linear scan divided by a logarithm.

questions.prompt: Which edge-weight assumption guarantees correctness of standard Dijkstra’s algorithm on every finite directed graph, using permanent finalization when a vertex is extracted?

answers.explanation: With nonnegative weights, extending a path cannot lower its weight. This makes it safe to finalize the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance.
Negative edges can invalidate an already finalized distance.

answers.text: The graph has at least one positive edge.
answers.explanation: One positive edge gives no guarantee about the remaining edges.
Degrees do not make the greedy distance invariant valid.

answers.text: The sum of all edge weights is nonnegative.
answers.explanation: A nonnegative total does not rule out a negative edge that breaks finalization.
This suffices for finite shortest-path distances, but standard Dijkstra can still fail with a negative edge.

answers.text: Every edge weight is an integer.
answers.explanation: Negative integers can break the algorithm just as negative real weights can.

answers.text: Every directed cycle has strictly positive total weight.
answers.explanation: Even an acyclic graph with a negative edge can break permanent finalization.

answers.text: All edges leaving the source are nonnegative.
answers.explanation: A later negative edge can still produce a shorter path to an already finalized vertex.

answers.text: There is at most one negative edge.
answers.explanation: A single negative edge is enough to defeat the correctness guarantee.

questions.prompt: For powers of two, let $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$ with $T(1)=1$. What is the tight asymptotic bound?

answers.explanation: Each of the $\log_2 n$ internal recursion levels costs $n$ in total. The leaves add $n$, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$.
The top-level work alone grows linearly.
The subproblem sizes halve; the recurrence does not generate exponentially many leaves in n.
There are logarithmically many levels, but each costs linear total work.
This misses the linear work repeated at every internal level.
The per-level cost is n and the depth is logarithmic, not linear.
Even the root contributes more work than this.
There is one logarithmic factor for the depth; the per-level work contributes no second logarithm.
Halving gives logarithmic depth, not double-logarithmic depth.
That exponent corresponds to three half-size recursive subproblems; this recurrence has two.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?

answers.text: Items with equal keys keep their original relative order.
answers.explanation: Stability preserves input order within each group of equal keys. It says nothing by itself about time or extra space.
That is a space property, not stability.

answers.text: Its output is always in descending order.
answers.explanation: Either ascending or descending sorting can be stable.

answers.text: It always runs in constant time.
answers.explanation: Stability concerns equal keys, not running time.

answers.text: It preserves the original order of all items.
answers.explanation: Items with different keys generally need to move relative to one another.

answers.text: It never moves an item whose key is duplicated.
answers.explanation: Equal-key items may move; only their relative order must remain.

answers.text: Its running time is the same on every input.
answers.explanation: Input-dependent running time and stability are separate properties.

answers.text: Items with equal keys end up in their original array positions.
answers.explanation: Positions may change when smaller or larger keys move around them.

answers.text: Items with unequal keys keep their original relative order.
answers.explanation: The requirement applies to equal keys; unequal keys must follow the sort order.

answers.text: It breaks equal-key ties by sorting a second field.
answers.explanation: An arbitrary second-field ordering may reverse the original order and violate stability.

questions.prompt: For a binary search tree with distinct keys, what order does an in-order traversal (left subtree, root, right subtree) produce?

answers.explanation: Every key in the left subtree is smaller than the root, and every key in the right is larger. Applying this recursively yields sorted order.
That would follow from right-root-left traversal.
The traversal does not track the chronology of insertion.
The search-tree invariant determines the ordering.
That is breadth-first traversal, not in-order traversal.

answers.text: Root first, then all remaining keys sorted.
answers.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree before the root.
In-order can visit an internal vertex before some leaves.

answers.text: Increasing order only if the tree is balanced.
answers.explanation: Balance affects performance and height, not the in-order ordering guarantee.

answers.text: Increasing order only if the tree is complete.
answers.explanation: The BST ordering invariant suffices; completeness is unnecessary.

answers.text: Increasing order separately within each depth level.
answers.explanation: The result is globally sorted across all levels, and vertices are not grouped by depth.

questions.prompt: In a hash table with separate chaining and $n$ stored keys, what is the worst-case time to search for a key, if hashing and each key comparison take $\Theta(1)$?

answers.explanation: All $n$ keys can collide into one bucket. Searching that chain can require $n$ comparisons. Expected constant time requires assumptions about hashing and load.
A search examines at most the stored chain, not exponentially many candidates.
Each key in a chain needs at most one comparison during an ordinary search.
Even computing the hash requires constant time.
This confuses expected performance under suitable assumptions with the worst case.
A chain is not a balanced search tree; it can contain every key.
There is no worst-case guarantee that chains stop at square-root length.

answers.text: Constant time whenever the load factor is at most 1.
answers.explanation: A small average bucket size does not prevent all keys from colliding into a single bucket.

answers.text: Logarithmic time if all stored keys are distinct.
answers.explanation: Distinct keys can have identical hash values.

answers.text: Constant time if the hash function is deterministic.
answers.explanation: Determinism does not prevent collisions; the worst case may still scan all keys.

questions.prompt: In a nonempty binary min-heap with distinct keys, which position is guaranteed to contain the minimum key?

answers.explanation: Every parent has a smaller key than its children. Following parent links shows that the root is no greater than any other key.
A leaf has no minimum guarantee.
Depth does not determine the minimum; the root is minimum.
Only the root is guaranteed to dominate every other key.
A heap does not have the in-order sorting property of a binary search tree.
Left-to-right position does not sort heap keys.

answers.text: The first child of the root.
answers.explanation: The root has a smaller key than that child.
That child is minimum only among the two child roots, not the entire heap.

answers.text: The median position in the array representation.
answers.explanation: Heap array order describes the complete tree, not sorted key order.

answers.text: The last position before the leaves begin.
answers.explanation: Internal positions below the root can still have larger keys than their ancestors.

questions.prompt: In a doubly linked list, you already hold a reference to a node. What is the worst-case time to unlink it, including updating head or tail if necessary, but excluding searching for it and freeing memory?

answers.explanation: Only a fixed number of neighboring links and possibly the head or tail references need to change.
Unlinking does not compare pairs of nodes.
Only local pointer changes are required.

answers.text: It is impossible without copying the list.
answers.explanation: The predecessor and successor links allow local removal.
Searching could be linear, but the question supplies the node reference.
No tree search or logarithmic walk is needed.
The number of changed pointers is independent of list length.

answers.text: Constant time only for nodes at the head.
answers.explanation: An interior node has predecessor and successor pointers, so it also takes constant time.

answers.text: Constant time only if the list is circular.
answers.explanation: Ordinary head and tail boundary cases still require only a fixed number of changes.

answers.text: Linear time because all later nodes change index.
answers.explanation: A linked list does not store a contiguous array of indices that must be shifted.

questions.prompt: Which abstract data type directly provides first-in, first-out removal?

answers.explanation: A queue removes the earliest inserted item that has not yet been removed.
A stack is last in, first out.
A set describes membership and does not require insertion-order removal.
A search tree is organized by keys, not arrival times.

answers.text: A min-priority queue ordered by task size.
answers.explanation: That removes the smallest task, which need not be the oldest.

answers.text: A max-priority queue ordered by task size.
answers.explanation: That removes the largest task, which need not be the oldest.
The map interface provides key-value access, not FIFO removal.

answers.text: A deque restricted to insertions and removals at the same end.
answers.explanation: Using the same end gives LIFO behavior. Opposite ends can implement FIFO.
Operation speed does not change LIFO ordering into FIFO.

answers.text: A sorted set ordered by item value.
answers.explanation: Value order need not match insertion order.

questions.prompt: An initially empty stack receives push(A), push(B), push(C), then two pop operations. Which values do the pops return, in order?

answers.explanation: A stack is last in, first out. C is on top, and B is immediately beneath it.
That is the order a FIFO queue would return.
The oldest item is not popped first from a stack.
C remains above B after the three pushes.
After popping C, B is still on top of A.
B cannot be popped while C remains above it.
Each pop removes the returned item; A was inserted only once.
Pop removes C, so the second operation returns B.
The first pop must return C, and removed elements cannot be popped again.
After removing C, the stack still contains A and B.

questions.prompt: Which condition is equivalent to a finite undirected simple graph being bipartite?

answers.text: It has no cycle of odd length.
answers.explanation: A two-coloring alternates colors around each cycle, so all cycles must be even. Conversely, if there are no odd cycles, distance parity gives a consistent two-coloring in each component.
A triangle has all degrees even but is not bipartite.
A connected graph may contain an odd cycle.
Edgeless graphs are bipartite, but many graphs with edges are too.

answers.text: It has no cycle of even length.
answers.explanation: A triangle has no even cycle but is not bipartite.

answers.text: It has no cycles of any length.
answers.explanation: Acyclicity is sufficient but not necessary; an even cycle is bipartite.

answers.text: It has an even number of vertices.
answers.explanation: A triangle plus an isolated vertex has even order but is not bipartite.
A five-cycle is triangle-free but not bipartite.

answers.text: Every connected component has an even number of vertices.
answers.explanation: A component can have odd order and still be bipartite, such as a three-vertex path.

answers.text: Every vertex belongs to at most one odd cycle.
answers.explanation: Even one odd cycle prevents a two-coloring.

questions.prompt: How many edges does the complete undirected simple graph $K_n$ have?

answers.explanation: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices contributes one edge. There are n choose 2 such pairs.
Each vertex connects to every other vertex, so the count is generally quadratic.
That is a tree’s edge count, not a complete graph’s.
This counts ordered pairs and includes pairs of a vertex with itself.
This counts every undirected edge in both directions.
This includes n extra diagonal pairs, corresponding to forbidden loops.
Complete graphs generally have quadratic rather than linear edge counts.
That counts a complete graph on n−1 vertices.
Every vertex has n−1 neighbors, not n−2.
The binomial count already includes every allowed edge; there is no extra edge.

questions.prompt: An undirected forest has $n$ vertices and $c$ connected components. How many edges does it have?

answers.explanation: Each component is a tree. If component $i$ has $n_i$ vertices, it has $n_i-1$ edges. Summing gives $n-c$.
Each component contributes one fewer edge than vertices, not one more.
Components contribute additively, not multiplicatively.
A forest has only linearly many edges.
This is the connected case c=1; every additional component reduces the edge count by one.
A tree contributes one fewer edge than vertices, not two fewer.
The number of components alone does not determine the internal edges.
The sum of c tree edge counts subtracts c, with no additional edge.
This subtracts one too many; summing n_i−1 gives exactly n−c.

answers.text: $n-c$ only if no vertex is isolated.
answers.explanation: An isolated vertex is a one-vertex tree and contributes zero edges, so the formula still holds.

questions.prompt: A finite directed graph has a topological ordering exactly when it satisfies which condition?

answers.explanation: A topological ordering places the tail of every edge before its head. A directed cycle makes this impossible; repeatedly removing an indegree-zero vertex orders any DAG.

answers.text: Every vertex has the same outdegree.
answers.explanation: Equal outdegrees neither prevent directed cycles nor ensure an ordering.
Strong connectivity with multiple vertices entails directed cycles.

answers.text: It has more edges than vertices.
answers.explanation: The edge count alone does not characterize topological orderability.

answers.text: Its underlying undirected graph has no cycle.
answers.explanation: That is sufficient but unnecessary: an acyclic orientation of a triangle admits an ordering.
Isolated vertices can appear anywhere in a topological ordering.
A nonempty finite DAG must have an indegree-zero vertex.

answers.text: It has at least one vertex of indegree zero.
answers.explanation: Another component can still contain a directed cycle.

answers.text: It has no directed cycle of length two.
answers.explanation: Longer directed cycles also prevent topological ordering.

answers.text: Its vertices can be ordered by nondecreasing indegree.
answers.explanation: Sorting by indegree does not necessarily place every tail before its head.

answers.explanation: Every edge has two endpoints, so summing degrees counts each edge twice.

The degree sum is twice the edge count, not half.

answers.text: $2|E|$ only if the graph is connected.

answers.explanation: A tree is connected and acyclic. Removing a leaf and its one edge gives an induction proving $|E|=|V|-1$.
That is one edge too many for a tree; a connected graph with n edges has a cycle.

That is the sum of degrees, which counts each edge twice.
A connected graph on n vertices needs at least n−1 edges.

answers.text: $n-1$ only when the tree is binary.

questions.prompt: Which statement defines membership of a decision problem in NP?

answers.text: Every yes-instance has a polynomial-size certificate verifiable in deterministic polynomial time.
answers.explanation: NP concerns efficient verification of yes-certificates. It does not require efficient deterministic search for those certificates.

answers.text: It cannot be solved by any algorithm.
answers.explanation: NP problems are decidable; exhaustive certificate search is possible.

answers.text: It requires non-polynomial time on every input.
answers.explanation: NP does not mean non-polynomial, and P is contained in NP.

answers.text: Its output must be a number.
answers.explanation: A decision problem has a yes/no output.

answers.text: Both yes- and no-instances must have polynomial-time verifiable certificates.
answers.explanation: This describes membership in NP intersect coNP, a stronger requirement than NP alone.

answers.text: A deterministic algorithm solves it in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: That defines P and is sufficient, but is not the definition of all NP problems.

answers.text: A polynomial-time verifier may use certificates of unbounded length.
answers.explanation: NP bounds certificate length polynomially in input size.

answers.text: Every no-instance has a polynomial-size certificate verifiable in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: That is the certificate characterization of coNP.

answers.text: At least one yes-instance has an efficiently verifiable certificate.
answers.explanation: The guarantee must cover every yes-instance and reject every certificate for each no-instance.

answers.text: A polynomial-time verifier accepts every certificate for a yes-instance.
answers.explanation: Only the existence of an accepting certificate is required; invalid certificates may be rejected.

questions.prompt: What does undecidability of the general halting problem mean?

answers.text: No algorithm always terminates and correctly decides, for every program and input, whether that program halts.
answers.explanation: Undecidability rules out a total, universally correct decider. Particular programs can still be analyzed, and simulation recognizes halting when it occurs.
Many programs halt; the obstacle is a universal decision procedure.

answers.text: No specific program can be proved to halt.
answers.explanation: Termination can be proved for many particular programs.
Simulation is possible, but it may itself run forever when the simulated program does.

answers.text: Every halting question requires exponential time.
answers.explanation: Undecidability is stronger than an exponential lower bound: no total decider exists.

answers.text: There is no algorithm that recognizes halting cases.
answers.explanation: Simulation recognizes a halting case by eventually observing termination.

answers.text: Only very large programs can fail to halt.
answers.explanation: Even a tiny unconditional infinite loop need not halt.

answers.text: A decider exists if it may take arbitrarily long but finite time on every input.
answers.explanation: That would still be a total decision algorithm, which undecidability rules out.

answers.text: No restricted programming language has a decidable halting problem.
answers.explanation: Some restricted languages or finite-state systems do have decidable halting problems.

answers.text: Simulation decides both halting and nonhalting by waiting long enough.
answers.explanation: Any finite wait is inconclusive when a program has not halted yet; it may halt later.

questions.prompt: Under polynomial-time many-one reductions, what two conditions make a decision problem NP-complete?

answers.text: It is in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: Membership supplies efficiently verifiable yes-certificates. NP-hardness says that solving this problem efficiently would solve every problem in NP efficiently.

answers.text: It is impossible to solve and impossible to verify.
answers.explanation: NP-complete problems are decidable and have polynomial-time verifiable yes-certificates.

answers.text: It uses polynomial space and has a numeric output.
answers.explanation: Those conditions do not define NP-completeness.

answers.text: It takes exponential time on at least one particular machine.
answers.explanation: A slow implementation does not establish a complexity lower bound or completeness.

answers.text: It is in P, and it reduces to an NP problem.
answers.explanation: These conditions do not establish NP-hardness.

answers.text: It is in NP, and it reduces to every problem in NP.
answers.explanation: The hardness direction is reversed: every NP problem must reduce to it.

answers.text: It is NP-hard, with no membership requirement.
answers.explanation: NP-hardness alone does not imply membership in NP.

answers.text: It is in NP, and some problem in NP reduces to it.
answers.explanation: An arbitrary easy NP problem can reduce to it; hardness requires all NP problems or a known NP-hard one.

answers.text: It is in coNP, and every NP problem reduces to it.
answers.explanation: This gives NP-hardness and coNP membership, but does not establish the required NP membership.

answers.text: It is in NP, and it is not known to have a polynomial-time algorithm.
answers.explanation: Lack of a known algorithm is not proof of NP-hardness.

questions.prompt: Why does $\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}$ hold?

answers.text: A polynomial-time decider can act as a verifier that ignores the certificate.
answers.explanation: For a problem in P, run its deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. It accepts exactly the yes-instances, regardless of the supplied certificate.

answers.text: NP means problems outside polynomial time.
answers.explanation: NP means nondeterministic polynomial time; it does not exclude P.

answers.text: Every problem can be solved in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: This is false; decidable problems exist outside P.

answers.text: All NP problems are already known to be in P.
answers.explanation: Whether P equals NP is unresolved.

answers.text: A verifier is allowed exponential time.
answers.explanation: An NP verifier must run in polynomial time.
P includes decision problems with both yes- and no-instances.

answers.text: The certificate may contain an arbitrarily long computation.
answers.explanation: NP certificates must have polynomial length.

answers.text: The verifier can accept without inspecting the input.
answers.explanation: It must still distinguish yes- and no-instances; running the decider does that.
Membership in P does not imply NP-hardness.

answers.text: Deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial time are proven equal.
answers.explanation: Only containment is known in general; equality is an open question.

The given cost is already Θ(N) steps; there is no additional factor of b in this statement.
